adversarial_test_results.prompt:
For most of the nineteenth century, the movement of trains along a single line of railway depended on a mixture of timetable rules and human memory. A stationmaster would note the departure of each train in a ledger, then telegraph the next station to announce that the line ahead was clear. This arrangement worked well enough on quiet branches, but on busy routes the margin for error was small and the consequences were severe. Engineers began to look for a mechanical arrangement that would make it impossible for two operators to grant permission for opposing movements at the same time.

The first practical answer was the block system. The line was divided into sections, and each section was guarded by a signal box. Before a train could enter a section, the signalman at the entrance had to obtain a release from the box at the far end. A pair of telegraph instruments, linked by a single wire, carried the necessary messages. The instruments were built so that the two signalmen had to cooperate in a fixed sequence: a release could only be given after the previous train had been formally reported clear. If either man tried to skip a step, the needle refused to move.

Later designs added a locking frame beneath the levers. Bars of steel were cut and drilled so that one lever could not be pulled unless certain others were already in the correct position. The frame was, in effect, a small mechanical computer made of iron. It stored the state of the section in the positions of its bars, and it refused any combination that would put two trains on a collision course. Signal engineers regarded the frame as the heart of the installation, and they spent long hours in drafty cabins adjusting the fit of the locking bars until every movement ran smoothly.

The men who worked these boxes had little formal training. They learned the sequence of bells by ear and the habits of the timetable by memory. One superintendent, asked how he trained new staff, said that the only reliable method was to stand behind them for a month and correct every mistake at once. The work was repetitive, the cabins were cold, and the hours were long, yet the record was remarkably good. Collisions on lines fitted with the newer apparatus became rare, and the companies that adopted it found that insurance rates fell.

By the early twentieth century the mechanical frame had reached a high degree of refinement, and its principles passed almost unchanged into the electrical systems that followed. Relay circuits copied the logic of the locking bars, and the language of the signal box, with its releases, its sections and its clearances, survived into an age of colour light signals and automatic detection. What began as a way of passing a message down a wire had become a general method for preventing any operator from making a dangerous choice.
